content: The text provided is a list of references from various studies and articles related to oral contraceptives, transdermal contraceptive patches, vaginal rings, and their associated risks, benefits, and pharmacokinetics. 1. A cohort and case-control analysis was conducted to evaluate the use of oral contraceptives containing levonorgestrel before and after 1995. The findings were published in the BMJ in 2000, volume 321, pages 1190–1195. 2. Jick SS and Hernandez RK investigated the risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolism in women using oral contraceptives containing drospirenone compared to those using levonorgestrel-containing oral contraceptives. This case-control study utilized U.S. claims data and was published in the BMJ in 2011, volume 342, article d2151. 3. Jick SS, Kaye JA, Russmann S, and Jick H assessed the risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolism in women using a contraceptive transdermal patch versus oral contraceptives containing norgestimate and 35 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol. The results were published in Contraception in 2006, volume 73, pages 223–228. 4. Lidegaard O, Edstrom B, and Kreiner S conducted a five-year national case-control study on oral contraceptives and venous thromboembolism. The study was published in Contraception in 2002, volume 65, pages 187–196. 5. Parkin L, Sharples K, Hernandez RK, and Jick SS performed a nested case-control study based on the UK General Practice Research Database to evaluate the risk of venous thromboembolism in users of oral contraceptives containing drospirenone or levonorgestrel. The findings were published in the BMJ in 2011, volume 342, article d2139. 6. Todd J, Lawrenson R, Farmer RD, Williams TJ, and Leydon GM re-analyzed the MediPlus database to examine venous thromboembolic disease and combined oral contraceptives. The study was published in Human Reproduction in 1999, volume 14, pages 1500–1505. 7. Van Hylckama Vlieg A, Helmerhorst FM, Vandenbroucke JP, Doggen CJ, and Rosendaal FR explored the venous thrombotic risk of oral contraceptives, focusing on the effects of estrogen dose and progestogen type. The results of the MEGA case-control study were published in the BMJ in 2009, volume 339, article b2921. 8. Vasilakis-Scaramozza C and Jick H assessed the risk of venous thromboembolism associated with cyproteroneor levonorgestrel-containing contraceptives. The study was published in The Lancet in 2001, volume 358, pages 1427–1429. 9. Ziller M, Ziller V, Haas G, Rex J, and Kostev K analyzed patient data from German gynecological practices to evaluate the risk of venous thrombosis in users of hormonal contraceptives. The findings were published in the Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 2014, volume 289, pages 413–419. 10. Lidegaard O, Nielsen LH, Skovlund CW, Skjeldestad FE, and Lokkegaard E conducted a Danish cohort study from 2001 to 2009 to assess the risk of venous thromboembolism associated with oral contraceptives containing different progestogens and estrogen doses. The study was published in the BMJ in 2011, volume 343, article d6423. 11. Dunn N, Thorogood M, Faragher B, de Caestecker L, MacDonald TM, McCollum C, et al. investigated the relationship between oral contraceptives and myocardial infarction in the MICA case-control study. The results were published in the BMJ in 1999, volume 318, pages 1579–1583. 12. Gronich N, Lavi I, and Rennert G conducted a population-based cohort study to evaluate the higher risk of venous thrombosis associated with drospirenone-containing oral contraceptives. The study was published in the CMAJ in 2011, volume 183, pages E1319–E1325. 13. Heinemann LA, Lewis MA, Thorogood M, Spitzer WO, Guggenmoos-Holzmann I, and Bruppacher R conducted a case-control study on oral contraceptives and the risk of thromboembolic stroke. The findings were part of the International Study on Oral Contraceptives and Health of Young Women and were published in the BMJ in 1997, volume 315, pages 1502–1504. 14. Kemmeren JM, Algra A, and Grobbee DE performed a meta-analysis on third-generation oral contraceptives and the risk of venous thrombosis. The study was published in the BMJ in 2001, volume 323, page 131. 15. Lewis MA conducted the Transnational Study on Oral Contraceptives and the Health of Young Women, presenting methods, results, new analyses, and the healthy user effect. The findings were published in Human Reproduction Update in 1999, volume 5, pages 707–720. 16. Lewis MA, Heinemann LA, Spitzer WO, MacRae KD, and Bruppacher R examined the use of oral contraceptives and the occurrence of acute myocardial infarction in young women. The results were part of the Transnational Study on Oral Contraceptives and the Health of Young Women and were published in Contraception in 1997, volume 56, pages 129–140. 17. Lidegaard O studied the influence of thrombotic risk factors when prescribing oral contraceptives in a control-only study. The findings were published in Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica in 1997, volume 76, pages 252–260. 18. Lidegaard O and Kreiner S conducted a case-control study on cerebral thrombosis and oral contraceptives. The study was published in Contraception in 1998, volume 57, pages 303–314. 19. Lidegaard O, Lokkegaard E, Jensen A, Skovlund CW, and Keiding N investigated thrombotic stroke and myocardial infarction associated with hormonal contraception. The study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2012, volume 366, pages 2257–2266. 20. Rosenberg L, Palmer JR, Rao RS, and Shapiro S evaluated the risk of myocardial infarction associated with low-dose oral contraceptive use. The study was published in the Archives of Internal Medicine in 2001, volume 161, pages 1065–1070. 21. Tanis BC, van den Bosch MA, Kemmeren JM, Cats VM, Helmerhorst FM, Algra A, et al. examined the relationship between oral contraceptives and the risk of myocardial infarction. The study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2001, volume 345, pages 1787–1793. 22. The World Health Organization conducted an international, multicenter case-control study on ischemic stroke and combined oral contraceptives. The findings were published in The Lancet in 1996, volume 348, pages 498–505. 23. The World Health Organization also conducted a similar study on acute myocardial infarction and combined oral contraceptives, with results published in The Lancet. 24. Yang L, Kuper H, Sandin S, Margolis KL, Chen Z, Adami HO, et al. investigated reproductive history, oral contraceptive use, and the risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke in a cohort study of middle-aged Swedish women. The study was published in Stroke in 2009, volume 40, pages 1050–1058. 25. Aedo AR, Landgren BM, Johannisson E, and Diczfalusy E conducted pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic investigations with monthly injectable contraceptive preparations. The study was published in Contraception in 1985, volume 31, pages 453–469. 26. Fotherby K, Benagiano G, Toppozada HK, Abdel-Rahman A, Navaroli FA, Ramos-Cordero R, et al. conducted a preliminary pharmacological trial of the monthly injectable contraceptive Cycloprovera. The study was published in Contraception in 1982, volume 25, pages 261–272. 27. Garza-Flores J studied the pharmacokinetics of once-a-month injectable contraceptives. The findings were published in Contraception in 1994, volume 49, pages 347–359. 28. Garza-Flores J, Rodriguez V, Perez-Palacios G, Virutamasen P, Tang-Keow P, Konsayreepong R, et al. conducted a multicentered pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic study of once-a-month injectable contraceptives, focusing on different doses of HRP112 and Depoprovera. The study was published in Contraception in 1987, volume 36, pages 441–457. 29. The World Health Organization Task Force on Long-Acting Systemic Agents for Fertility Regulation conducted a multicentered phase III comparative study of two hormonal contraceptive preparations given once a month by intramuscular injection. The study focused on contraceptive efficacy and side effects and was published in Contraception in 1988, volume 37, pages 455–466. 30. Haiba NA, el-Habashy MA, Said SA, Darwish EA, Abdel-Sayed WS, and Nayel SE conducted a clinical evaluation of two monthly injectable contraceptives and their effects on some metabolic parameters. The study was published in Contraception in 1989, volume 39, pages 619–632. 31. Kesseru EV, Aydinlik S, Etchepareborda JJ, and Kaufmann J conducted a multicentered, two-year, phase III clinical trial of norethisterone enanthate 50 mg plus estradiol valerate 5 mg as a monthly injectable contraceptive. The study was published in Contraception in 1991, volume 44, pages 589–598. 32. Meng Y-X, Jiang HY, Chen AJ, Lu FY, Yang H, Zhang MY, et al. studied hemostatic changes in women using a monthly injectable contraceptive for one year. The findings were published in Contraception in 1990, volume 37, pages 1–20. 33. Abrams LS, Skee D, Natarajan J, Wong FA, Lasseter KC, et al. investigated the multiple-dose pharmacokinetics of a contraceptive patch in healthy women participants. The study was published in Contraception in 2001, volume 64, pages 287–294. 34. Audet M-C, Moreau M, Koltun WD, Waldbaum AS, Shangold GA, Fisher AC, et al. evaluated the contraceptive efficacy and cycle control of a transdermal contraceptive patch versus an oral contraceptive in a randomized trial. The study was published in JAMA in 2001, volume 285, pages 2347–2354. 35. Boonyarangkul A and Taneepanichskul S compared cycle control and side effects between a transdermal contraceptive patch and an oral contraceptive in women older than 35 years. The study was published in the Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand in 2007, volume 90, pages 1715–1719. 36. Burkman RT reviewed the transdermal contraceptive patch as a new approach to hormonal contraception. The findings were published in the International Journal of Fertility in 2002, volume 47, pages 69–76. 37. Cole JA, Norman H, Doherty M, and Walker AM examined venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, and stroke among transdermal contraceptive system users. The study was published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2007, volume 109, pages 339–346. 38. Devineeni D, Skee D, Vaccaro N, Masserella J, Janssens L, LaGuardia KD, et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of a transdermal contraceptive patch and an oral contraceptive. The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2007, volume 47, pages 497–509. 39. Dittrich R, Parker L, Rosen JB, Shangold GA, Creasy GW, Fisher AC evaluated three transdermal norelgestromin/ethinyl estradiol doses in a randomized, multicenter, dose-response study. The study was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2002, volume 186, pages 15–20. 40. Helmerhorst FM, Cronje HS, Hedon B, Shangold GA, Fisher AC, Creasy GW compared the efficacy, cycle control, compliance, and safety of a contraceptive patch versus an oral contraceptive. The study was published in the International Journal of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 2000, volume 70, supplement 1, page 78. 41. Jick S, Kaye J, Li L, and Jick H provided further results on the risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolism in users of the contraceptive transdermal patch compared to users of oral contraceptives containing norgestimate and 35 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol. The study was published in Contraception in 2007, volume 76, pages 4–7. 42. Jick SS and Jick H studied cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in users of four hormonal contraceptives: levonorgestrel-containing oral contraceptives, norgestimate-containing oral contraceptives, desogestrel-containing oral contraceptives, and the contraceptive patch. The study was published in Contraception in 2006, volume 74, pages 290–292. 43. Jick SS and Jick H examined the contraceptive patch in relation to ischemic stroke and acute myocardial infarction. The findings were published in Pharmacotherapy in 2007, volume 27, pages 218–220. 44. Jick SS, Kaye J, Russmann S, and Jick H assessed the risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolism in women using a contraceptive transdermal patch and oral contraceptives containing norgestimate and 35 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol. The study was published in Contraception in 2006, volume 73, pages 223–228. 45. Pierson RA, Archer DF, Moreau M, Shangold GA, Fisher AC, Creasy GW compared follicular development and ovulation in normal cycles and after an intentional dosing error between Ortho Evra and oral contraceptives. The study was published in Fertility and Sterility. 46. Radowicki S, Skorzeqska K, and Szlendak K evaluated the safety of a transdermal contraceptive system compared to an oral contraceptive. The study was published in Ginekologia Polska in 2005, volume 76, pages 884–889 (in Polish). 47. Smallwood GH, Meador ML, Lenihan JP, Shangold GA, Fisher AC, Creasy GW assessed the efficacy and safety of a transdermal contraceptive system. The study was published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2001, volume 98, pages 799–805. 48. Urdl W, Apter D, Alperstein A, Koll P, Schonian S, Bringer J, et al. examined contraceptive efficacy, compliance, and factors related to satisfaction with once-weekly transdermal contraception compared to oral contraception. The study was published in the European Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology and Reproductive Biology in 2005, volume 121, pages 202–210. 49. White T, Ozel B, Jain JK, and Stanczyk FZ studied the effects of transdermal and oral contraceptives on estrogen-sensitive hepatic proteins. The findings were published in Contraception in 2006, volume 74, pages 293–296. 50. Zieman M, Guillebaud JG, EW, Shangold GA, Fisher AC, Creasy GW analyzed pooled data on contraceptive efficacy and cycle control with the Ortho Evra/Evra transdermal system. The study was published in Fertility and Sterility in 2002, volume 77, supplement 1, pages s13–s18. 51. Van den Heuvel MW, van Bragt AJM, Alnabawy AKM, and Kaptein MCJ compared ethinyl estradiol pharmacokinetics in three hormonal contraceptive formulations: the vaginal ring, the transdermal patch, and an oral contraceptive. The study was published in Contraception in 2005, volume 72, pages 168–174. 52. Ahrendt HJ, Nisand I, Bastianelli C, Gómez MA, Gemzell-Danielsson K, Urdl W, et al. evaluated the efficacy, acceptability, and tolerability of the combined contraceptive ring, NuvaRing, compared with an oral contraceptive containing 30 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol and 3 mg of drospirenone. The study was published in Contraception in 2006, volume 74, pages 451–457. 53. Bjarnadottir RI, Tuppurainen M, and Killick SR compared cycle control with a combined contraceptive vaginal ring and oral levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol. The study was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2002, volume 186, pages 389–395. 54. Dieben TO, Roumen FJ, and Apter D assessed the efficacy, cycle control, and user acceptability of a novel combined contraceptive vaginal ring. The study was published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2002, volume 100, pages 585–593. 55. Duijkers I, Killick SR, Bigrigg A, and Dieben TO conducted a comparative study on the effects of a contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing) and an oral contraceptive on carbohydrate metabolism and adrenal and thyroid function. The study was published in the European Journal of Contraception and Reproductive Health Care in 2004, volume 9, pages 131–140. 56. Duijkers I, Klipping C, Verhoeven CH, and Dieben TO studied ovarian function with the contraceptive vaginal ring or an oral contraceptive in a randomized study. The findings were published in Human Reproduction in 2004, volume 19, pages 2668–2673. 57. Elkind-Hirsch KE, Darensbourg C, Ogden B, Ogden LF, and Hindelang P found that contraceptive vaginal ring use in women has fewer adverse metabolic effects than an oral contraceptive. The study was published in Contraception in 2007, volume 76, pages 348–356. 58. Magnusdottir EM, Bjarnadottir RI, Onundarson PT, Gudmundsdóttir BR, Geirsson RT, Magnusdóttir SD, et al. conducted a comparative study on the contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing) and hemostasis. The study was published in Contraception in 2004, volume 69, pages 461–467. 59. Massai R, Makarainen L, Kuukankorpi A, Klipping C, Duijkers I, and Dieben T studied the combined contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing) and bone mineral density in healthy premenopausal women. The findings were published in Human Reproduction in 2005, volume 20, pages 2764–2768. 60. Milsom I, Lete I, Bjertnaes A, Rokstad K, Lindh I, Gruber CJ, et al. evaluated the effects on cycle control and body weight of the combined contraceptive ring, NuvaRing, versus an oral contraceptive containing 30 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol and 3 mg of drospirenone. The study was published in Human Reproduction in 2006, volume 21, pages 2304–2311. 61. Oddsson K, Leifels-Fischer B, de Melo NR, Wiel-Masson D, Benedetto C, Verhoeven CH, et al. conducted a one-year randomized trial comparing the efficacy and safety of a contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing) with a combined oral contraceptive. The study was published in Contraception in 2005, volume 71, pages 176–182. 62. Sabatini R and Cagiano R compared profiles of cycle control, side effects, and sexual satisfaction of three hormonal contraceptives. The study was published in Contraception in 2006, volume 74, pages 220–223. 63. Timmer CJ and Mulders TM studied the pharmacokinetics of etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol released from a combined contraceptive vaginal ring. The findings were published in Clinical Pharmacokinetics in 2000, volume 39, pages 233–242. 64. Tuppurainen M, Klimscheffskij R, Venhola M, and Dieben TO conducted a comparative study on the combined contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing) and lipid metabolism. The study was published in Contraception in 2004, volume 69, pages 389–394. 65. Veres S, Miller L, and Burington B compared the vaginal ring and oral contraceptives. The study was published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2004, volume 104, pages 555–563. 66. O’Connell KJ, Osborne LM, and Westoff C measured and reported weight change for women using a vaginal contraceptive ring versus a low-dose oral contraceptive. The study was published in Contraception in 2005, volume 72, pages 323–327. 67. Fine PM, Tryggestad J, Meyers NJ, and Sangi-Haghpeykar H evaluated the safety and acceptability of using a contraceptive vaginal ring after surgical or medical abortion. The study was published in Contraception in 2007, volume 75, pages 367–371. 68. Vestergaard P, Rejnmark L, and Mosekilde L assessed fracture risk in very young women using combined oral contraceptives. The study was published in Contraception in 2008, volume 78, pages 358–364. 69. Vestergaard P, Rejnmark L, and Mosekilde L also examined oral contraceptive use and the risk of fractures. The findings were published in Contraception.
